newsitem.title: USA: No McVeigh fingerprints found on certain evidence.
newsitem.headline: No McVeigh fingerprints found on certain evidence.

text.p: Timothy McVeigh's fingerprints could not be found on several pieces of evidence that could tie him to the Oklahoma City bombing, a government witness testified on Thursday.

The admission by fingerprint specialist Louis Huff was a blow to the prosecution and a rare plus for the defence team, which maintains that authorities arrested the wrong man for the April 19, 1995 bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in Oklahoma City which killed 168 people.
Huff, taking the stand for the third time in the high- profile trial, said McVeigh's prints were not found on the rental form for the Ryder truck that prosecutors say was used in the bombing.

He said his prints were also not found at Elliott's Body Shop in Junction City, Kansas, where the truck was allegedly rented, despite dismantling the counter and taking it back to the FBI laboratory in Washington D.C.

No testimony will be heard on Friday because of a juror's request to attend her son's college graduation out of state. Federal Judge Richard Matsch admonished the jury to avoid publicity about the case over the long break.
"We're running in good time here. You have heard a lot of evidence from the government. There's more to go, but we're getting there in terms of witnesses offered by the prosecution," the judge said.
"You have to wait until you've heard it all, including evidence in contradiction of what you've heard," Matsch said.

Huff said he also did not find any of McVeigh's fingerprints on a key that prosecutors said fit the rental truck, nor on storage units allegedly rented to hold the bomb components. Nor were any prints of McVeigh's found in the motel rooms where prosecutors allege he stayed in the days before the bombing.
Under direct testimony, Huff said someone could touch something and not leave fingerprints.

Huff testified that McVeigh's prints were found on a receipt for ammonium nitrate, which prosecutors say was purchased to make the bomb. The receipt was found in the home of Terry Nichols, McVeigh's alleged co-conspirator who will be tried separately.

In a setback for the defence, the judge allowed prosecutors to admit a T-shirt that McVeigh was allegedly wearing when he was arrested. "The tree of liberty must be replenished from time to time with the blood of patriots and tyrants," was written on the back of the T-shirt, quoting Thomas Jefferson.
The judge admitted other clothing items, but said he would make a decision later on whether to admit earplugs that the prosecution says McVeigh wore during the bombing.

The defence had hoped to keep the clothes out. It has claimed McVeigh's clothing may have been contaminated with explosive residue due to improper handling by authorities. A jail employee testified that McVeigh's clothes were placed in a brown paper bag and kept in a room to which various people had access.
The defence also presented evidence that two people charged with explosives possession were held in the jail the month before McVeigh's arrest.
Huff admitted that other than wearing gloves he took no special precautions with his own clothing to avoid contamination while he handled McVeigh's clothing.

"Do you have protocols to avoid contamination?" defence attorney Cheryl Ramsey asked Huff. "We're establishing protocols as we speak," said Huff, who conceded that the new protocols were not in place in 1995.
In other testimony, an expert identified the vehicle used in the bombing as a Ryder truck allegedly rented by McVeigh.

"I believe that there was only one vehicle used in the Oklahoma City bombing. That vehicle, built for and sold to Ryder, had a specific and unique vehicle identification number," said Edward Paddock, who had worked for 34 years for Ford Motor Co., which manufactured the Ryder truck.
